For Rubric 2 the c2 G2 and G5 REASONS were corrected (one too narrow, one overstated) and no c2 LABEL changed. Ratification by the maintainer is PENDING and no run counts until it is given: the c2 labels are judgement, not construction. Open for ratification, raised by the held-out run (runs/2026-10-17-r1-kiro-cli-claude-sonnet-5): it passed c2 G3 and G4 where this key fails them. Those two labels were set by reading c2, not by an edit to it, so they are exactly the kind this file flags as judgement. Both were left as they stand, and the maintainer decides; changing either is a key change, which re-runs both passes under shipBar rule 4. c7 and c8 (added for Rubric 2): c7's labels are judgement, set by reading it, exactly as c2's and c4's were, and need the same ratification; c8's follow from c7's and the mutation. RATIFIED 2026-10-19 by the maintainer. c2's G3 and G4 stand as fail: the held-out run passed them without arguing against the key (its findings were on D2, D3 and D5), and relabelling forbids a relabel that only a run asked for. c7's five gate labels and its D1 floor of 3 stand, on the same reading standard c2's and c4's were held to; c8's follow. c1.mutation: Step 1 also closes the bridge when each turn's prompt settles, clears the cached bridge promise, and removes the resume branch of resolveSession(), so every turn takes the divergence branch and advertises a fresh bridge in a new session/new. The in-scope list, the approach, criterion 3 and a new verification step were written to agree, so the mutation reads as a deliberate design change rather than an oversight, and is internally consistent. Its contract is still open, and could not be closed: useResume is computed before resolveSession(), so a per-turn session reset sends a delta prompt to an empty session, and no wording of this mutation decides that without rewriting turn planning. Reading as deliberate is what makes c1 a test of D3 and the reject row; the open contract is what makes G1 fail. Both follow from the edit, not from a run. Goal 3 ('the per-child bridge URL invariant (§5e.3) is preserved'), the root cause ('kiro learns the bridge URL only once, at session/new'), criterion 4 (the §5e.3 tests pass unchanged) and the out-of-scope 'bridge URL lifetime model' line were left alone. §5e.3 records that kiro keeps its client for the server named pi pointed at the first port even across session/new, so every bridged call after the first turn hits a closed port; and dropping resume breaks Goal 3's 'resume behaves as before'.

why.mustQuoteOneOf: The defect is a contradiction, so a finding may quote either side: the per-turn bridge text, or Goal 3, criterion 4 and the out-of-scope line, which the mutation left promising one bridge URL per child.
why.outcome: reject by construction, not by vote: the mutation overturns the documented §5e.3 decision without proposing to supersede it, which is the rubric's reject row and D3's anchor 1. Pass 5 (both runs reject, D3 1) prompted the relabel; the rubric text decides it. c1 is also the case that exposed the missing precedence rule (review item 8): it has G1 fail AND a reject condition, and the rubric's gates section used to force revise unconditionally, so the held-out run answered revise by reading that line literally. The rubric now says reject outranks revise, which makes this key reachable from the text and keeps a reject verdict on a spec with a failed gate valid.
why.D3: 1 by construction: the mutation overturns the documented 5e.3 decision without proposing to supersede it, which is anchor 1's second clause, and the outcome table's reject row reads from the same fact. Not 2: one contradiction left unaddressed is anchor 2, and overturning a documented decision is listed a row below it. BOTH runs of Rubric 3's first pair wrote this out in prose, naming the decision and that the spec does not propose to supersede it, and then scored D3 2 and answered revise. That is the third time the set has seen one shape: a finding that describes anchor N scored at N+1, after c6's D1 in the same pair and c1's own outcome in the pass before it. Nothing in Rubric 3 bound a written finding back to the row it came from, so the number was free to drift one row generous while the prose stayed right, and the anti-softening sentence that did exist covered only the outcome's tone. Rubric 4 states the binding in both tables and gives it a step: a dimension's score is never higher than the lowest row its own findings describe, the outcome is never softer than the findings, and Review procedure step 8 reads the findings back against both tables and corrects step 6's numbers where they disagree. The label is unchanged. What changed is that a verdict asserting a row and the row above it at once is now a rule violation rather than an inconsistency a reviewer is free to hold.
why.G1: A per-turn bridge has no closed contract at this ref, and the failing case is one the spec names: Goal 3 promises that resume behaves as before, and the mutation removes the resume branch of resolveSession() without touching turn planning. useResume is computed by planAcpTurn() before resolveSession() runs, and promptContent is still chosen by useResume (src/acp-transport.ts at 61bb96f, the turn body: buildDeltaPrompt when useResume, else buildPromptFromContext). So on a follow-up turn the spec sends a delta prompt into the fresh session the divergence branch just created, and says nothing about it: it neither replaces the delta prompt nor argues the case cannot arise. That is Rubric 2's G1 'Also fails, with no choice offered' bullet exactly: the change bypasses what existing code relies on for a named case and decides nothing in its place. Rubric 1's Fails list named only specs offering a choice, which is why both runs of the post-review pair passed this gate while finding the defect elsewhere (D2, D3); the label did not move, the gate's list now reaches it. The label follows the code, checked at 61bb96f, not a run. SETTLED by Rubric 2's pair: the pi/us.anthropic.claude-opus-5 run failed this gate and reached this reason independently, naming planAcpTurn/useResume, buildDeltaPrompt and the history-less session, from the code and not from this file. So the label is now re-derived from the construction by a reviewer as well as by its author, which is what relabelling asks of a label a run has questioned, and it stands. What did not hold is the gate's reach: the kiro-cli/gpt-5.6-terra run of the same pair passed G1 while filing the defect as D3 and D2, so three of the four models that have seen c1 stop at the contradiction. Rubric 3 answers that in two places, neither of which touches this label: G1's Not G1 bullet now says that finding the D2 or the D3 does not answer G1, and the Review procedure makes listing the cases the spec names a step of its own, before any gate is decided.

c2.source: real: dual-host-pi-gsd.md, frozen from the maintainer's untracked working copy on 2026-10-17

why.G1: 'Mechanics (pick the lightest that satisfies Step 0)' leaves the wiring shape (a package.json pointing at the entry, or a re-exporting index.ts) to the implementer, and that shape is what the documented enable step tells users to create. Option C's 'skip a bare-pi-only convenience' does not name what is skipped.
why.G4: Criterion 4 ('does not alter or break GSD's own extension set') names no evidence, and no Verification plan step produces any.
why.D5: No target version, no CHANGELOG line, and no workaround for current users (launch under bare pi).
why.D1: Step 0 verifies the loader contract against a named, versioned build (@opengsd/gsd-pi v1.22.0), so the diagnosis is strong even though its evidence is external.
why.G2: Three claims are credited to sources the spec never names, and Rubric 2's G2 fails an unnamed source on being unnamed, whether or not a matching document exists: 'referenced in older steering notes' (a version claim about external software, notes not named), 'Negative control first (per repo engineering rule)' (no rule named), and 'ASCII-only in any host-read string ... per repo convention' (no convention named; none is written anywhere in the repository at 61bb96f). Any one fails the gate. CORRECTED for Rubric 2: the Rubric 1 reason said the engineering-rule half was wrong because docs/releasing.md ('Citing a test, and when a fix may waive one') states the revert-run-restore procedure. That file does describe the procedure, but not as a general engineering rule and never under the name negative control, and c2 names no source at all; a reviewer who finds a similar document does not repair the citation. Both runs of the post-review pair failed this half, one after reading docs/releasing.md, and both were right. The label (fail) is unchanged; only the reason was too narrow.
why.G3: 'confirm it fails (provider not registered / load error)' gives two outcomes and no mechanism, and the GSD-home test it names builds the wiring itself, so nothing says why it would fail before the change. SETTLED for Rubric 4, and the label does not move. Both runs of Rubric 3's first pair passed this gate, which makes c2's G3 the set's second both-miss after the feature column, and the cause is the gate's reach rather than the label. Rubric 3's Fails list named a reason that is not the defect, a test described only as passing, and a run with no stated expectation for the unchanged side; this control is none of those. It states a reason, and the reason is in the right area. What it does is offer two of them, and name a check whose own setup supplies what the pre-change failure is attributed to. Rubric 4 adds both to the Fails list and explains them beneath it: a reason naming one mechanism or another has not settled which, and an unsettled mechanism is not a stated one; and a control whose setup builds the thing whose absence before the change is supposed to make it fail exercises the setup rather than the code as it stands. Neither sentence quotes c2 (test/rubric-anchors.test.ts), and neither reaches the six cases this key passes on G3: in c1, c4, c5 and c6 the stated reason is a single property of the code at the ref (a referenced handle, an unreferenced child), and in c7 and c8 it is a single mechanism chain in the unchanged reader. The label was ratified on 2026-10-19 and stands.
why.G5: The transport item ('The transport/parsing internals (ACP vs chat) - unaffected by host scoping.') gives a reason and no disposition: it names no spec, issue or owner and does not say the item is dropped or unchanged. That item alone fails the gate. CORRECTED for Rubric 2: the Rubric 1 reason also counted the credential item, but that item opens with 'unchanged', which is one of G5's listed dispositions, so it overstated. The cmux item names its owner (GSD-owned). Pass 1 corrected c4 for the same defect, so the same reading applies here.

c3.mutation: The fail-first step is gone: the unit test is still described, but nothing says to run it against the unfixed bridge.ts, and the manual reproduction runs only after the change.

c4.source: real: acp-print-mode-exit.md, frozen from the maintainer's untracked working copy on 2026-10-17, then corrected over eight calibration passes (README, 'How the set was corrected'). Each correction was a finding both runs, or one run with a citation, made against the frozen copy, checked against the code at 61bb96f before anything changed. The same base edits were applied to c1, c3, c5 and c6, and each mutation was kept, except c1's: pass 4 removed the step it mutated, so it was rebuilt on the same contradiction. The exemplar and the false-fail control.

why.G1: Pass under Rubric 2's wider list as well as Rubric 1's. The triggers are fixed (right after listen() resolves; once session/new resolves; the existing finally). Each case the spec names is decided: during a turn, a bridged call mid-turn, the chat transport, interactive pi, and the startup wait. The change raises no error of its own (unref() and setChildKeepalive() do not throw) and adds no name or signature: serveBridgeHttp() returns the same handle. It does bypass something existing code relies on, the referenced listener holding the loop open through the startup wait, and the spec names that wait and replaces the hold with an explicit setChildKeepalive(), which is what the 'Also fails, with no choice offered' bullet asks of a bypass. c3 and c6 share this Approach verbatim, and c5 differs only by its G2 misspelling, so the same reading holds for all three.
why.G4: Criterion 6 is a documentation criterion under Rubric 2's G4: it names CHANGELOG.md's 0.4.1 Fixed section and package.json, and says what each must contain, so it needs no Verification plan step. Criteria 1 to 5 are behaviour criteria and each has a step (the live regression for 1 and 2, the negative control and startup-gate test for 3, the full suite for 4 and 5). c3's criterion 6 and its steps for criteria 4 and 5 are byte-identical to c4's, so c3 G4 passes for the same reason; Rubric 1's G4 let one run fail c3 and pass c4 on that text.
why.G5: Every item has a disposition. The credit-metering item names a follow-up spec and owner; host scoping names docs/specs/dual-host-pi-gsd.md and nothing else, which is a disposition under Rubric 2's G5 clause that a named spec, issue or owner needs no reason beside it (c4 is the only case with a bare named target, and the Rubric 1 wording left 'with the reason' able to reach it); the idle-timeout item says unchanged, no follow-up; the session_shutdown teardown item says no follow-up and gives two reasons. Rubric 2's G5 counts a bare 'no follow-up' as a disposition and 'not needed' as a reason beside it, so that item passes. c3, c5 and c6 carry the same Out of scope list and pass G5 the same way. CLARIFIED for Rubric 3: the credit-metering item gives its owner as a role, not as a person, and one run of Rubric 2's pair failed c6's G5 on exactly that. Rubric 2's G5 settled whether a named target has to resolve and said nothing about how specific the name has to be. Rubric 3 says an owner may be a person, a role or a team, and that what fails is an item naming no destination of any kind. The label is unchanged in all four cases that share this list.
why.D5: Criterion 6 now names the release section, the workaround and the test citation docs/releasing.md requires of a ### Fixed bullet, so 3 is the floor, not the expected score.

c5.mutation: The provenance commit 6ea0510 becomes 6ea0517, which does not exist, and serveBridgeHttp is spelled serveBridgeHTTP at all four mentions.

why.G2: Lint catches both with no model (see lint.mustName). The blind reviewer must also catch at least one, which is the check that it opens what a spec cites rather than trusting it.
why.G5: pass: every out-of-scope item carries a disposition, and c5's mutation touches only a commit and a symbol. The held-out run failed it anyway, because it could not resolve the sibling spec c5's out-of-scope item names and treated an out-of-scope item whose named target does not exist as having no disposition. That is a G2 finding, and the run also raised it under G2, so one citation was counted against two gates. The rubric now says G5 judges the sentence and not the citation. c4 carries the same line and the same run passed its G5, which is the evidence that this was wording and not the reviewer.

Rubric 2's pair hit exactly that: the pi/us.anthropic.claude-opus-5 run filed the D1 finding this case asks for, on this sentence, with the right tag and the right score, and omitted the period. The full stop is removed here, and quoteMatching in shipBar now states the rule for every such string. No label moved; the text quoted is the same text.
why.D1: 2 by construction: the mutation hedges the cause, offering it as what the author expects is happening where the evidence to settle it is present in the spec, which is anchor 2's second clause. Not 3: anchor 3 needs a mechanism traced to code, and a hedged cause is not a settled one. BOTH runs of Rubric 3's first pair described the hedge accurately and scored D1 3, which is the same anchor-row off-by-one as c1's D3 in the same pair; see that reason for the shape and for Rubric 4's answer to it. why.G5: Passes, and it is the reading Rubric 3 made explicit. c6 carries c4's Out of scope list, whose first item sends the work to a follow-up spec with an owner given as a role rather than as a person. The kiro-cli/gpt-5.6-terra run of Rubric 2's pair failed G5 on that, reading 'a named spec, issue or owner' as requiring a specific target; Rubric 2's G5 answered whether a named target must resolve and said nothing about how specific the name must be. Rubric 3 says an owner may be a person, a role or a team, so the item has a disposition and the label stands on the construction: the mutation that makes c6 touches the Root cause bullets only, and c4's Out of scope list is unchanged in it.

The gaps are still tied to the same code. Two back-references ('measured above') become 'described above', so the spec stays consistent with itself. why.D1: Feature anchor 2, 'current behaviour asserted, not measured', by construction: the mutation removes every command, output and ref from the Problem and changes nothing else. Not 1: there is a problem statement beyond the goal. Not 3: tying each gap to code is the second half of anchor 3, whose first half is 'Measured'. c7 and c8 differ only in the measurement, so a reviewer that scores them the same is not reading D1's feature column. BOTH runs of Rubric 2's pair scored c7 and c8 at D1 4, so the pair failed featureColumn on its first outing, and this is the only miss in the set's history that no reviewing model got right. The reason is not a gate's wording: row 4 reads as a list of credits, and c8 satisfies its second half (each gap tied to the code that produces it) while satisfying none of its first. Rubric 3 says so outside the table: for a feature spec measurement is a precondition of a 3 or a 4, tying gaps to code carries no score on its own, and the evidence the spec presents is what is scored rather than whether its conclusions turn out to be true. The Review procedure also makes listing that evidence a step of its own, which caps D1 at 2 when the list comes out empty. The label is unchanged; what changed is where a reviewer is told to look.
why.mustQuoteOneOf: A finding about the missing measurement may quote the Problem heading, the asserted subsection's heading, or either asserted paragraph. CORRECTED after Rubric 4's probe, and the correction is the rubric's, not a run's. The rubric's Findings section says a finding about something missing quotes the nearest heading, and what is missing from c8 is the measurement from the whole Problem section, so '## Problem' is the heading that rule names. It was not in this list. Both probe runs filed a correct c8 D1 finding - right tag, right score of 2, reasoning straight from Rubric 3's measurement precondition - and both were scored a miss on the quote alone; run A's quote was exactly '## Problem'. A rule that penalises a reviewer for following the rubric's own instruction measures quoting style, not review quality, which is the same defect Rubric 3 fixed in six strings' terminal punctuation. Adding the heading follows from the rubric as written and from how c8 was built (the mutation strips the measurement from the Problem section and changes nothing else), which is the standard shipBar.relabelling sets. RATIFIED by the maintainer for Rubric 5, which is what capabilityMatched's 'a probe never amends the rubric on its own' asks for: the probe is what exposed the defect, and the amendment is derived without it. The rubric's Findings rule names the nearest heading, c8's mutation strips the measurement from the whole Problem section and changes nothing else, so '## Problem' is the heading that rule names whether or not any run quoted it. DECLINED, same decision: run B quoted a verbatim sentence from the same section that is not one of the three listed, and its finding was also correct. Widening the list to any sentence in the section would make the rule vacuous; widening it to that sentence is tuning the key to a run. It is recorded in runs/SCORE.md and not acted on.

shipBar.independence: Each run is a fresh session per case. The two runs must differ in session; at least one must also differ in harness or model from the other.
shipBar.blind: Calibration reviewers are given lint's notes and never lint's result. In production lint runs first and a lint failure is never reviewed; calibration reviews every case, including the two lint fails, so that the reviewer half can be measured on its own. That means withholding the verdict, not the notes. The rubric's Review procedure step 3 is 'Work through every item lint listed under notes (G2 reviewer half)', and G2 divides itself the same way: its script half owns 'a repo path that does not exist at the ref', its reviewer half opens with what lint listed WITHOUT failing. Rubric 3's first pair ran with no lint output at all, so step 3 had no input and the boundary between G2's two halves was left for the reviewer to guess. The two runs guessed opposite ways, across all six of their gate disagreements and the only false fail the pair produced. The runner now writes lint's notes object, and nothing else from lint, into each session's input directory, and the prompt names it as step 3's input while forbidding a self-run. c3 is why the result itself stays withheld: its whole construction is a lint G3 failure the reviewer has to reach on its own.
shipBar.mustCatch: Every case meets its outcome, every gate label, every dimension threshold, and its mustQuoteOneOf, in both runs. A revise on c4 is a false fail and counts as a miss.
shipBar.agreement: The two runs agree on every gate decision for every case (8 cases x 5 gates = 40 decisions since Rubric 2; 30 before c7 and c8). Any disagreement means the rubric wording is ambiguous: fix the wording and re-run both, do not pick a winner. Gate agreement is not the whole bar: c7 and c8 are labelled pass on all five gates, so ten of the 40 decisions are ones a reviewer that passed everything would agree on. See featureColumn.
shipBar.featureColumn: The bar is not met unless both runs separate c7 from c8 on D1: c7 at 3 or more, c8 at 2 or less. mustCatch already requires this of each run; it is a rule of its own because the 40 gate decisions do not measure it. c7 and c8 are labelled pass on all five gates, so the pair widened the set by ten gate decisions and no fail, and the feature column is the only thing it discriminates. Without this rule a run could meet the stated bar having never read D1's feature column, which is the reason the pair exists. The two cases differ only in whether the current behaviour is measured, so a run that scores them the same on D1 has not read it. Rubric 2's pair did exactly that, both runs, which is why Rubric 3 moved the feature column's precondition out of the anchor table and into prose beside it and made listing the Problem's evidence a step of the Review procedure. No reviewing model satisfied this rule for the set's first eight runs. Rubric 3's own first pair then met it, both runs scoring c7 at 4 and c8 at 2, and Rubric 4's probe met it again: the first time a change to the rubric's text closed a miss that no model had got right.
shipBar.relabelling: A miss is fixed in the rubric's wording. The answer key may be relabelled only when the new label follows from how the case was BUILT - the mutation that was applied, or the text as frozen, checked against the code at ref - and never because a run said so. A relabel re-runs both passes; the runs that prompted it do not count towards the new key. Pass 8 broke this rule: c1's G1 was relabelled because both runs failed it, and the same two runs were then declared to meet the new key with nothing re-run. That result is withdrawn (see runs/SCORE.md).
shipBar.blobs: A run is tied to a rubric by blob, not by the Rubric: number, because a wording fix that keeps the meaning does not bump the number while 'Changing this rubric' still re-runs calibration. Every run directory carries RUN.json with the git blob sha of spec-review/rubric.md and of this file as they stood when it was scored, plus the case blobs. A run counts towards the ship bar only when both match the committed blobs at the merge commit. This is what makes a stale run visible instead of plausible.
shipBar.capabilityMatched: The two runs should be at a comparable capability level. The bar measures agreement between them, so pairing a strong reviewer with a weak one cannot distinguish an ambiguous rubric from a reviewer that could not do the task, which is the one thing rule 4 has to tell apart. A deliberately cheap model may be run as a non-gating robustness probe, recorded in the run's NOTES.md; a probe never amends the rubric on its own and never counts as one of the two runs.
shipBar.heldOut: A model that took part in a pass, or in a wording fix made in response to a pass, is in the tuning loop and cannot be one of the two runs. As of Rubric 2 that excludes six: claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6-astra (passes 1 to 8); claude-sonnet-5 (the held-out run whose misses drove the item 7, 8 and 20 wording fixes); claude-opus-4.8 (it reviewed the bus spec from a worktree that shared this branch's object database, so it could read this file; see 'Reviewer independence' in the README); us.anthropic.claude-fable-5-1 and gpt-5.6-sol (the post-review pair, whose misses drove Rubric 2's G1, G2 and G4 fixes); and gpt-5.6-terra and us.anthropic.claude-opus-5 (Rubric 2's pair, whose misses drove Rubric 3's D1, G1 and G5 fixes and the quoteMatching correction). That was eight as of Rubric 3. claude-opus-4.7 and us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-6-v1 join it as Rubric 3's first pair, so it is ten, and the next pair needs an eleventh and a twelfth. They are spent whatever that pair turned out to measure: this rule excludes a model that TOOK PART IN A PASS, not only one whose misses moved a word, and four of their six disagreements moved the runner instead (aliasResolves, blind). Ten models across four attempts have not cleared the bar; the best gate agreement a gating attempt has recorded is 36/40, and the best in the set is the 38/40 of Rubric 4's non-gating probe, so the supply of comparable top-tier models is now the binding constraint on criterion 12, and if the next pair misses it is the bar's shape rather than the rubric's wording that needs the argument. The model that drafted Rubric 2 is claude-opus-5-5, already excluded. Rubric 3 was drafted by us.anthropic.claude-opus-5, which its own run has just spent, so the draft excludes nothing that was not already excluded. SETTLED for Rubric 5: the rule is the broad one, and Rubric 4's narrowing is withdrawn. Rubric 4 narrowed the reach to a model whose output moved the rubric's TEXT, on the ground that the harness is not what the bar measures. That reading is unsafe for the one thing this rule exists to stop. Under it, a pair whose misses are attributed to the runner becomes eligible again, so the same two models can be re-run after each harness fix until session variance puts a pair over the bar - and a bar cleared on the nth re-roll of the same two models measures the rolling, not the rubric. The broad rule has no such path: taking part in a pass spends a model, whatever that pass turned out to measure. It costs the pool two models the narrow rule would have returned, claude-opus-4.7 and us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-6-v1, four of whose six disagreements moved the runner rather than a word of the rubric, and that cost is the point of the rule. Nothing changes in practice: Rubric 4's two fixes answer those two models' misses directly - c2's G3, which both passed, and the anchor-row off-by-one, which both committed - so they were inside the tuning loop under either reading, and spent has stayed at ten throughout. They may be re-run as a non-gating probe (capabilityMatched), which is the tightest test of those two fixes available: the two models that committed the defects, asked again under the corrected harness and the corrected wording. That probe has run, at 38 of 40, and a probe never amends the rubric on its own and never counts as one of the two runs. Spent stays at ten, and the gating pair still needs an eleventh and a twelfth.
shipBar.quoteMatching: A mustQuoteOneOf string is matched as a substring of a finding's line, so it must not end in sentence punctuation. Rubric 2's pair cost a correct finding a miss on a single period: the quote was verbatim but for the full stop the key had kept. Keep these strings free of a terminal full stop, comma or semicolon rather than normalising at match time, because the matcher stays a plain substring test that way and the string in this file is exactly what a reviewer has to produce. Six strings lost a terminal full stop for Rubric 3, five in c1 and one in c6; the text quoted is the same text and no label moved. The rule is held by test/calibration-ship-bar.test.ts, which also checks that every string is still findable in its case, so trimming one into something no reviewer could quote fails too.
shipBar.aliasResolves: An aliased citation resolves from the reviewer's own clone. The runner copies each alias target into the session clone at the path the spec cites, so G2 is answered from the checkout exactly as every other citation is, and spec-lint.mjs is handed the same mapping on its command line, so the gate's two halves see one world. The alias used to be a file in the input directory under its basename, plus a prompt sentence saying where to read it: that sentence says where the content is and not that the citation resolves. Run B of Rubric 3's pair read the filesystem instead, found docs/specs/dual-host-pi-gsd.md absent at 61bb96f, and failed G2 on it in c1, c3, c4 and c6; c4's verdict is that one finding and nothing else, which is the only false fail in the pair. Held by test/calibrate.test.ts, where placing the file under its basename again fails one test and only that test.
shipBar.clone: A reviewer gets a git clone, never a worktree. git worktree add shares the object database, so this file is one git show away from a reviewer in a worktree of this branch.
shipBar.deterministic: test/spec-lint.test.ts holds the lint expectations above in CI, and test/rubric-anchors.test.ts holds that the rubric quotes no case.
